intro: Many people picture Satan as a horned monster and think of demons as the stuff of scary movies. The ancient texts are quieter and more interesting than that. In the Hebrew Bible, satan is a word for an adversary. In Job, "the satan" stands in God's own court. Much later, the New Testament uses Satan and the devil as names for one enemy of God. This unit follows how that change happened.

Your guide is Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Bible's ancient languages. In Demons (2020) and The Unseen Realm (2015), he sorted the Bible's dark powers into three groups: the rebel of Eden, the rulers over the nations, and demons, which he read as the spirits of the giants in 1 Enoch. You will read his case alongside the main readings that differ from it, from Jewish and Christian readers and from other scholars.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain what satan means in Hebrew and why the word "the" matters. You will compare readings of Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28. You will trace names like Belial and Mastema, read 1 Enoch 15 and the Gospel stories in Mark, and explain the two goats of the Day of Atonement. You will also practice reading these stories with care.
bigQuestion: How did ancient texts picture the powers that stand against God, and how did Heiser explain where they came from?

timeline.t: Isaiah begins to prophesy in Jerusalem; Isaiah 14 later mocks the king of Babylon

Revelation 12:9 calls the dragon the old serpent, the devil and Satan

test.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean?
test.why: Satan is a Hebrew word for an adversary or opponent, used for angels, kings and soldiers.

test.q: Why did Heiser read "the satan" in Job as a title, not a name?
choices: It is written in Greek letters
It appears only in the Septuagint
It has the article "the", which names usually do not take
test.why: In Demons (2020) Heiser pointed to the Hebrew article ha-: "the satan" describes a role, as "the judge" does.

test.q: Who does the satan accuse in Zechariah 3?
test.why: Zechariah 3:1 shows the satan at the right hand of Joshua the high priest, accusing him.

test.q: Which poem is addressed to the king of Tyre?
test.why: Ezekiel 28 is a lament over the king of Tyre, who is pictured in Eden. Isaiah 14 is about the king of Babylon.

test.q: What did Heiser see behind Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28?
choices: Human kings pictured through the story of the Eden rebel
The spirits of the dead giants
test.why: Heiser read both poems as aimed at real kings but patterned on the story of a divine rebel cast down from Eden.

test.q: Which Greek word gave English the word devil?
test.why: Devil comes from diabolos, slanderer, which the Septuagint used for ha-satan in Job.

test.q: In which book is Mastema the chief of the spirits?
test.why: Jubilees, from about 160 BCE, names Mastema as chief of the evil spirits.

test.q: Which verse gathers the names dragon, old serpent, devil and Satan?
test.why: Revelation 12:9 gives all four names for one figure who deceives the whole world.

test.q: In Heiser's three groups, which group did he tie to the Genesis 6 story?
test.why: Heiser read demons as the spirits of the giants born when the sons of God took human wives in Genesis 6.

test.q: What does 1 Enoch 15 say about the giants' spirits?
choices: They became evil spirits living on the earth
They were sent away on the Day of Atonement
They became the rulers of the nations
test.why: 1 Enoch 15:8–12 says the spirits that came out of the dead giants became evil spirits on the earth.

test.q: Which Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 names spirit beings Israel sacrificed to?
test.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 uses shedim, which the Septuagint translated as demons.

test.q: How does Mark 5 end for the man from the tombs?
choices: He follows Jesus by boat to Capernaum
He goes home and tells his story in the Ten Cities
test.why: In Mark 5:19–20 Jesus sends the man home to his friends, and he tells his story in the Decapolis.

test.q: How do the Gospels treat healing the sick and freeing people from spirits?
choices: As things only priests could do
As things that never happened in Galilee
As two separate things, as in Mark 1:32–34
test.why: Mark 1:32–34 lists the sick and those troubled by demons as two groups, keeping healing and freeing apart.

test.q: What happened to the goat for Azazel on the Day of Atonement?
choices: It carried the people's sins into the wilderness
It was kept in the temple courtyard
It was offered on the altar
It was given to the high priest's family
test.why: Leviticus 16:21–22 says the high priest confessed the sins over the living goat, and it was led into the wilderness.

test.q: Which view says demons are fallen angels who followed Satan?
choices: A common Christian view drawing on Revelation 12:9
test.why: Many Christians teach that demons are angels who joined Satan, pointing to Revelation 12:9. Heiser read them as the giants' spirits.

write.prompt: Where did ancient readers think the Bible's dark powers came from? Choose two or three passages from this unit, such as Job 1:6, Isaiah 14:12, 1 Enoch 15:8–12 or Mark 5:1–20. Explain what each text says, how Heiser read it, and how at least one other reader or tradition reads it differently.
tips: Name each text you cite with its book, chapter and verse.
Attribute every idea: "Heiser argued…", "many Christians read…", "Jewish readers see…".
Compare the readings fairly; you do not need to pick a winner.
Use the unit's terms, such as satan, divine council, Watchers and unclean spirit, and explain each one.
